extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy / Plato (general readers, philosophy students, instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Plato's Republic (Books VII–VIII) describing educational requirements for guardians/philosopher-kings and the characterization/origins/defects of five forms of government (aristocracy/timocracy/oligarchy/democracy/tyranny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to abstract and define the idea of the good
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate must be able to abstract and define rationally the idea of good, run the gauntlet of all objections, and be ready to disprove them, not by appeals to opinion but to absolute truth, never faltering at any step of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person cannot do this he knows only a shadow given by opinion and not by science; such a person is not fit to apprehend the idea of good or to rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest science
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is the coping-stone of the sciences and is set over them; no other science can be placed higher—the nature of knowledge can no further go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign dialectic to the highest natures; dialectic provides the standard by which rulers should be trained and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for rulers: surest, bravest, and fairest natures
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers should be chosen with preference given to the surest and the bravest, and, if possible, to the fairest; they should have noble and generous tempers and natural gifts that facilitate their education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is based on inborn temperaments and natural gifts, not merely social status; these dispositions make further education viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gifts required (keenness and rapid acquisition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such gifts as keenness and ready powers of acquisition are required, for the mind often faints from the severity of study more than the body from exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for quickness of understanding and appetite for intellectual toil; these gifts reduce dropout from rigorous study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good memory and love of sustained labour
rubrics_metrics.description: He should have a good memory and be an unwearied solid man who is a lover of labour in any line, or he will never endure the great amount of bodily exercise and the intellectual discipline required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endurance, steadiness, and a demonstrable enjoyment of sustained effort are indicators of suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid half-industrious or divided vocations
rubrics_metrics.description: The votary should not be half industrious and half idle (e.g., loving gymnastic and hunting but hating study), nor devote himself to opposite occupations which produce a lame nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: candidates who split commitments between demanding bodily pursuits and avoid intellectual labor are unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral integrity: intolerance of voluntary falsehood; shame at ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: A soul that hates voluntary falsehood and is indignant at lies, and that is ashamed when detected in ignorance, is preferable to one that is patient of involuntary falsehood and wallows in ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral sensitivity and intellectual honesty are required; toleration for ignorance or negligence is disqualifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful discrimination of virtues in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of temperance, courage, magnificence, and every other virtue, make careful distinctions between true sons and bastards; failing to discern leads to error in choices of rulers and friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each virtue specifically rather than assuming overall goodness; partial defects indicate unsuitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early childhood instruction in elements (calculation, geometry, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation and geometry and all other elements of instruction, which prepare for dialectic, should be presented to the mind in childhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce foundational abstract disciplines early so later dialectical synthesis is possible; but avoid forcing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject compulsion in learning; use amusement to find bent
rubrics_metrics.description: A freeman ought not to be a slave in acquisition of knowledge; bodily exercise when compulsory does no harm to the body, but knowledge acquired under compulsion obtains no hold on the mind—so let early education be a sort of amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational techniques should attract and intrigue children rather than coerce them; use play/attraction to reveal natural aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose children to managed danger/experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Children were to be taken to see the battle on horseback and, when no danger, brought close up and, like young hounds, have a taste of blood given them; the same practice may be followed in labours, lessons, and dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supervised experiences that test temperament and confer appropriate exposure to seriousness/violence; use such tests as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic trials as an important early test
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial of who is first in gymnastic exercises is one of the most important tests to which youth are subjected; after gymnastic training, those selected at twenty will be promoted and have their scattered learning brought together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical trials reveal endurance, discipline, and nature; use them as part of combination assessment alongside intellectual criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive mind as criterion of dialectical talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to see the natural relationship of sciences and a comprehensive mind is the great criterion of dialectical talent; the comprehensive mind is always the dialectical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ability to integrate knowledge across domains rather than narrow expertise alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection timeline and stages of training
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with comprehension and steadfastness, after military and other duties, at age thirty are chosen and proved by dialectic; suggested schedule includes ~5 years of intensive study, ~15 years of public office experience, and culmination at age fifty to behold the absolute good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training alternates concentrated study with long practical experience; final philosophical leadership comes after decades of preparation and tested public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: dangers of early/unchecked dialectic (lawlessness/eristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic can introduce lawlessness; students may become eristic—arguing for amusement, contradicting without seeking truth, and thus give philosophy a bad name unless introduced carefully and to orderly, steadfast candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard dialectical teaching with ethical formation and delayed exposure; distinguish truth-seeking dialecticians from mere debaters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must temper other dispositions (music with philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy tempered with music is the best guardian of virtue throughout life; without such tempering the guardian power is lost and the man will be drawn to avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend aesthetic/moral education with intellectual training to sustain virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal living and lack of private property for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors will place soldiers in houses common to all, contain nothing private or individual, and have no ordinary possessions of mankind; they receive maintenance but not private wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic separation of rulers from private accumulation is prescribed to prevent corruption and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-kings' motives: esteem right above honors
rubrics_metrics.description: True philosopher rulers despise worldly honors, esteem right and the honor that springs from right, and regard justice as the greatest good; they rule out of duty and order the State according to the absolute good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rulers' motives—those who seek honor for its own sake are inferior to those who value justice and right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of children from populace to be reared by the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The State will send out inhabitants above ten years and take possession of their children, unaffected by parental habits; these are to be trained in the laws and habits of the guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social engineering via upbringing aims to break prior corrupting influences and inculcate desired civic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as the ideal constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy (the government of the best/philosopher-kings) is presented as the best form; the man answering to it is the most just and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aristocracy as the normative standard against which others are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocracy (honour-based government) origin and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Timocracy arises from a mixture when fertility/sterility and human cycles produce imperfect succession; it values honour, military virtues, gymnastics and the chase rather than philosophy, and its rulers are contentious, ambitious, lovers of honour and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize timocracy by a predominance of spirited/passionate elements and reverence for martial honor over intellectual culture; it tends toward secret covetousness and hoarding of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy defined by property qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy rests on a valuation of property in which the rich have power and the poor are deprived; a sum of money is fixed as the qualification for citizenship and governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule is based on wealth, not ability or virtue; property thresholds exclude many capable citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects of oligarchy (rule by wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great defects include rule by wealth rather than skill (e.g., pilots chosen by property would shipwreck), division into two States (rich vs poor), incapacity to wage war effectively (fear of arming the masses), unwillingness to pay taxes, extremes of wealth and poverty, and the production of paupers and criminal elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess oligarchies by social fragmentation, moral decline, criminality, and incompetence in public functions caused by illegitimate selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of regime change: accumulation of gold leads to oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Timocracy degrades into oligarchy when accumulation of gold and secret hoarding become widespread; increasing love of money displaces love of virtue, leading to legal changes (property qualifications) and constitutional transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace constitutional decay via economic incentives and cultural devaluation of virtue; monetary accumulation is a key causal factor.
